    Chapter 8

    Passwords and Key Derivation

    🤔 Hackers just stole your website’s password database. Whether that’s a shrug or a catastrophe depends on one choice you made years ago.

    • ⏱️ ~5 min
    • 📚 9 sections
    • 🎮 7 interactive
    • ⭐ 280 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    8.1The password problem#

    A website needs to check your password every time you log in, but it should never store your actual password. Databases get stolen constantly; billions of account records have leaked over the years. And because people reuse passwords, one leaked password often unlocks email, banking and social media accounts too.

    So how can a site check a password it doesn't store? With a one-way hash. At sign-up, the site stores hash(password). At login, it hashes what you typed and compares.

    But how you hash matters enormously.

    ✔ section read

    8.2Password storage, from worst to best#

    Method What a thief gets after stealing the database Verdict
    Plaintext Every password, instantly ❌ Unforgivable
    Encrypted Every password, once they find the key (usually on the same server) ❌ Bad
    Fast hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) Most passwords in hours: GPUs test billions of guesses per second, and precomputed tables crack common passwords instantly ❌ Bad
    Fast hash + salt Precomputed tables no longer work, but billions of guesses per second still do ⚠️ Not enough
    Slow, salted password hash (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2) Only very weak passwords, and slowly ✅ Correct
    ✔ section read

    8.3Salt: stopping precomputed attacks#

    Attackers build giant lookup tables: "here's the hash of every common password." (A clever compressed version is called a rainbow table.) With unsalted hashes, cracking is just a lookup. Worse, users with the same password have the same hash, so cracking one cracks them all.

    A salt is a random value, unique to each user, mixed in before hashing:

    The salt isn't secret. It's stored right next to the hash. Its job is to make every hash unique, so attackers can't precompute anything and must attack each user separately.

    8.4Slow on purpose: key stretching#

    Hash functions like SHA-256 are designed to be fast, which is exactly wrong for passwords. A password hash should be deliberately slow and memory-hungry:

    • A real user logs in once and waits maybe a quarter of a second. Fine.
    • An attacker trying a billion guesses waits a billion quarter-seconds: about 8 years per account for that list.

    Memory-hardness matters too. Attackers use graphics cards (GPUs) and custom chips with thousands of tiny cores. If each guess needs, say, 64 MB of memory, those cores can't all run at once, because the chip doesn't have enough memory.

    Algorithm Year Slow? Memory-hard? Recommended settings (OWASP guidance) Notes
    Argon2id 2015 ✅ ✅ At least 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 thread ✅ First choice. Winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition.
    scrypt 2009 ✅ ✅ N=2¹⁷, r=8, p=1 ✅ Good
    bcrypt 1999 ✅ Partly Cost factor 10 or higher ✅ Good; widely supported. Only the first 72 bytes of a password count.
    PBKDF2 2000 ✅ ❌ 600,000 iterations with HMAC-SHA256 ⚠️ Use when regulations require it (FIPS)

    These settings get raised over time as computers get faster. Good systems re-hash a user's password with stronger settings the next time that user logs in.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Password hashing algorithms

    ✅ Use it
    Argon2id

    2015, PHC winner

    • Memory-hard: cripples GPUs and ASICs
    • Tunable memory, time and threads
    • Not FIPS-approved
    • Memory cost must be tuned for your servers
    Best for: First choice for new systems
    ✅ Use it
    scrypt

    2009

    • Memory-hard
    • In Python’s standard library
    • Parameters interact in confusing ways
    • Memory and time tied together
    Best for: Good alternative; crypto wallets
    👍 Situational
    bcrypt

    1999, Blowfish-based

    • Battle-tested for 25 years
    • Supported by every framework
    • Only the first 72 bytes count
    • Only partly memory-hard (4 KB)
    Best for: Existing systems; cost ≥ 10
    ⚠️ Legacy
    PBKDF2

    2000, iterated HMAC

    • FIPS-approved; everywhere
    • Simple
    • Not memory-hard: GPUs love it
    • Needs 600,000+ iterations
    Best for: When regulations require FIPS
    ❌ Avoid
    Fast hash (+salt)

    SHA-256, MD5…

    • Salt stops rainbow tables
    • Billions of guesses per second on a GPU
    Best for: Never for passwords

    8.6Pepper: an extra secret#

    A pepper is a secret value added to every password before hashing, stored separately from the database (for example, in a hardware security module or a separate config system). If only the database is stolen, the attacker can't even start guessing, because they lack the pepper.

    ✔ section read

    8.7Advice for humans: what makes a strong password#

    Length beats complexity. Each random character adds a little strength; each random word adds a lot.

    A common method is Diceware: pick words at random (using real dice) from a list of 7,776 words. Each word adds about 12.9 bits of entropy:

    Passphrase Entropy Example
    4 random words ~52 bits correct horse battery staple
    5 random words ~65 bits tundra pellet obtuse nimble gravy
    6 random words ~78 bits mango orbit fable crisp wagon ledge
    P@ssw0rd! ~0 bits One of the first guesses attackers try

    Best practices:

    • Use a password manager. It generates a different random password for every site, so one breach can't spread.
    • Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA). Even a stolen password isn't enough.
    • Prefer passkeys where available. They replace passwords with public-key cryptography (Chapter 16).

    📜 Clever use of hashing: "Have I Been Pwned." This service checks whether your password appeared in a breach without you sending it the password. Your browser hashes the password with SHA-1 and sends only the first 5 characters of the hash. The service returns all leaked hashes starting with those 5 characters (hundreds of them), and your browser checks for a match locally. The service never learns your password or even its full hash. This technique is called k-anonymity.

    8.8Key derivation functions (KDFs): one secret, many keys#

    A KDF turns one secret into one or more cryptographic keys. There are two kinds.

    1. Password-based KDFs turn a human password into an encryption key. These are the same slow algorithms as above (PBKDF2, scrypt, Argon2). Examples: password managers deriving the key that encrypts your vault, encrypted ZIP files, disk encryption unlocked by password, and WPA2 Wi-Fi (Chapter 15).

    2. HKDF (HMAC-based KDF) takes a secret that is already strong and random (such as the output of a key exchange) and expands it into several independent keys. It works in two steps:

    • Extract: concentrate the randomness into a fixed-size, uniformly random key.
    • Expand: stretch it into as many keys as needed, each with a different label ("info").

    TLS 1.3, Signal, the Noise protocol framework (used by WireGuard) and many other systems use HKDF.

    💡 Key idea: key separation. Never use the same key for two different purposes (for example, encryption and MAC). Derive separate keys with a KDF. If one use is ever compromised, the others stay safe.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Key derivation functions

    ✅ Use it
    HKDF

    Extract-then-Expand

    • Turns one strong secret into many independent keys
    • Used by TLS 1.3, Signal, Noise
    • Useless for passwords (it’s fast)
    • Input must already be high-entropy
    Best for: After key exchange
    ✅ Use it
    Password KDF

    Argon2, scrypt, PBKDF2

    • Makes a human password usable as a key
    • Slow on purpose
    • Weak passwords stay weak
    • Costs server CPU and RAM
    Best for: Password managers, encrypted archives, Wi-Fi
    ✔ section read

    8.9Hands-on with password hashing#

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python):

    Python
    # Argon2id (pip install argon2-cffi)
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()                       # sensible defaults: 64 MiB, 3 iterations, 4 threads

stored = ph.hash("correct horse battery staple")
print(stored)    # $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$...$...

print(ph.verify(stored, "correct horse battery staple"))   # True
try:
    ph.verify(stored, "Tr0ub4dor&3")
except Exception as e:
    print("Wrong password:", type(e).__name__)              # VerifyMismatchError
    Python
    # bcrypt (pip install bcrypt)
import bcrypt
stored = bcrypt.hashpw(b"correct horse battery staple", bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
print(stored)                                              # b'$2b$12$...'
print(bcrypt.checkpw(b"correct horse battery staple", stored))   # True
    Python
    # scrypt and PBKDF2 are built into Python's standard library
import hashlib, os

password = b"correct horse battery staple"
salt = os.urandom(16)

key1 = hashlib.scrypt(password, salt=salt, n=2**17, r=8, p=1,
                      maxmem=256*1024*1024, dklen=32)
key2 = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password, salt, 600_000)
print(key1.hex())
print(key2.hex())
    Python
    # HKDF: derive separate keys from one master secret
import secrets
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

master = secrets.token_bytes(32)
enc_key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"encryption").derive(master)
mac_key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None, info=b"authentication").derive(master)
print(enc_key != mac_key)   # True: same master, independent keys
